claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
Under standard processing, the W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation.
Under standard processing, the W–Cu composite develops interfacial voids.
Ti and Cr can serve as carbide-forming coating elements.
Depositing a thin Ti- or Cr-containing reactive coating during W–Cu fabrication will produce an in situ interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
The reactive coating will form a chemically compatible carbide or nitride layer at the W–Cu interface.
The interlayer will reduce the W–Cu interfacial energy.
The interlayer will mitigate deleterious interdiffusion at the W–Cu interface.
A carbide-forming coating can promote metallurgical bonding between a particle and a metal matrix by forming an interfacial carbide layer.
The reactive interlayer will reduce the driving force for phase separation in W–Cu under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The reactive interlayer will suppress interfacial void formation in W–Cu during processing and service.
The modified interface will preserve structural integrity and continuous thermal-transport pathways during service.
Interfacial phase separation and voiding degrade the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The treated W–Cu composite will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite after high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
Heat flux above 10 MW/m2 is relevant to service conditions for joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components.
The proposed interlayer remains applicable under irradiation levels typical of plasma-facing-component joints.
